lead: Aircraft spar webs and fuselage shear webs are made so thin that they buckle in shear well below the design load. Buckling is not failure: the wrinkled web carries the load as a field of diagonal tension, held in place by the flanges and the vertical stiffeners. Wagner's theory of the complete tension field gives the stress in the web, the extra compression in the flanges, the load in the stiffeners and the angle of the wrinkles.
prereq: You need: shear flow in a web between two booms from the idealisation chapter, and the idea of plate buckling under shear.

sections.h3: A buckled web still carries shear

blocks.text: A flat web of depth d and thickness t between two flanges carries a shear W as a shear flow q = W/d, a stress τ = W/(t d). Pure shear is the same as tension on one 45° diagonal and equal compression on the other. A thin web cannot carry much compression: at a critical shear stress τ<sub>cr</sub> it buckles into wrinkles along the tension diagonal. For a panel with simply supported edges, short side b and long side a:
τ<sub>cr</sub> = k<sub>s</sub> π² E (t/b)²/[12(1 − ν²)],   k<sub>s</sub> ≈ 5.35 + 4(b/a)²
blocks.where: τ<sub>cr</sub> is the shear buckling stress (N/mm²); E is Young's modulus (N/mm²); ν Poisson's ratio; t the thickness and b the shorter panel side (mm); a the longer side (mm); k<sub>s</sub> the shear buckling coefficient for simply supported edges.

blocks.text: For a 1 mm web τ<sub>cr</sub> is a few N/mm², far below the working stress. After buckling the compression diagonal carries almost nothing, and the shear is carried by tension along the wrinkles at an angle α to the flanges. If the web is so thin that the buckling stress is negligible, the field is a complete tension field: that is Wagner's idealisation. A beam whose web carries the whole shear without buckling is a shear-resistant web beam, and its flows are those of the earlier chapters.

Take a cantilever with tip load W, flanges a distance d apart, and vertical stiffeners at spacing b. Cut a vertical section through the web. The diagonal tension σ<sub>t</sub> acts on a strip of width d sin α, so its vertical component is σ<sub>t</sub> t d sin α cos α. That must equal W:

blocks.where: σ<sub>t</sub> is the diagonal tension stress (N/mm²); W is the shear force (N); t the web thickness and d the depth between flange centroids (mm); α the angle of the tension field to the flanges.

blocks.text: The horizontal component of the same field is W/tan α, a tension in the web that the two flanges must resist. Each takes half, as compression, on top of its bending load. At a distance z from the tip:
F<sub>T</sub> = W z/d − W/(2 tan α),   F<sub>B</sub> = −W z/d − W/(2 tan α)
blocks.where: F<sub>T</sub> and F<sub>B</sub> are the axial forces in the top and bottom flanges (N), tension positive, for a downward tip load with the top flange in tension; z is the distance from the load (mm).

blocks.text: On a horizontal cut the field pulls the flanges towards each other with a force σ<sub>t</sub> t sin²α per unit length. The stiffeners hold them apart, so each stiffener is a strut:
P = σ<sub>t</sub> t b sin²α = W b tan α/d
blocks.where: P is the compressive load in one stiffener (N); b is the stiffener spacing (mm).

sections.h3: The angle α and the flange bending

blocks.text: Statics does not give α. Wagner found it by minimising the strain energy of web, flanges and stiffeners: stiff flanges and stiffeners hold the field near 45°, flexible ones let it rotate. For a web of thickness t, flanges of area A<sub>F</sub> and stiffeners of area A<sub>S</sub>:

blocks.where: A<sub>F</sub> is the area of one flange (mm²); A<sub>S</sub> the area of one stiffener (mm²). Rigid flanges and stiffeners give tan α = 1, α = 45°.

blocks.text: Between stiffeners the field also pulls sideways on each flange, a distributed load σ<sub>t</sub> t sin²α = W tan α/d per unit length. The flange acts as a continuous beam over the stiffeners and carries a secondary bending moment W b² tan α/(12d) at each stiffener and half that midway between. It must be designed for this as well as its axial load.

Real webs buckle at a non-zero τ<sub>cr</sub>, so part of the shear is carried by the flat-web mechanism and part by tension. Semi-empirical incomplete tension field methods share the load between the two; Wagner's complete field is the limit, and it is conservative for the flanges and stiffeners.

figure.caption: The worked Wagner beam. The buckled web carries the 20 kN shear as tension along wrinkles at 40.9° to the flanges, σ<sub>t</sub> = 101.1 N/mm². The field compresses each flange by 11.56 kN on top of its bending load and turns every stiffener into a 12.98 kN strut.

A 20 kilonewton load acts down at the free end. Labels give the top flange force as 48.4 kilonewtons at 1.2 metres from the tip, the bottom as minus 71.6, and the stiffeners as 12.98 kilonewton struts. A box gives the diagonal tension as 101.1 newtons per square millimetre, the flange loss as 11.56 kilonewtons each and the secondary moment as 0.324 kilonewton metres.

examples.question: A cantilever beam has flanges 400 mm apart, each 500 mm² in area, a web 1 mm thick, and vertical stiffeners of 200 mm² every 300 mm. It carries a tip load of 20 kN. Take E = 70 GPa and ν = 0.33. Check that the web buckles, then use Wagner's complete tension field to find α, σ<sub>t</sub>, the flange forces 1.2 m from the tip, the stiffener load and the flange secondary bending moment.
steps: Nominal web shear: q = W/d = 20,000/400 = 50 N/mm, τ = 50 N/mm² in a 1 mm web.

Buckling: each panel is 300 × 400 mm, so b = 300 mm and k<sub>s</sub> = 5.35 + 4(300/400)² = 7.60. τ<sub>cr</sub> = 7.60 × π² × 70,000 × (1/300)²/(12 × (1 − 0.33²)) = 5.46 N/mm². It is about a ninth of the working stress, so a complete tension field is a fair model.
Diagonal tension: σ<sub>t</sub> = 2 × 20,000/(1 × 400 × sin 81.7°) = 40,000/(395.8) = 101.1 N/mm². At 45° it would be 100 N/mm².

Flanges at z = 1200 mm: bending gives W z/d = 20,000 × 1200/400 = 60,000 N; the field adds W/(2 tan α) = 11,560 N of compression to each. F<sub>T</sub> = 48,440 N (tension), F<sub>B</sub> = −71,560 N (compression).
Stiffener: P = W b tan α/d = 20,000 × 300 × 0.8651/400 = 12,976 N compression, a stress of 64.9 N/mm² in its 200 mm².
Flange secondary bending: W b² tan α/(12d) = 20,000 × 300² × 0.8651/(12 × 400) = 324,398 N·mm at each stiffener, 162,199 N·mm midway between.
examples.answer: α = 40.9°, σ<sub>t</sub> = 101.1 N/mm²; at 1.2 m F<sub>T</sub> = 48.4 kN and F<sub>B</sub> = −71.6 kN; each stiffener carries 12.98 kN; flange secondary moment 324 N·m at the stiffeners.

traps: Calling web buckling failure. The buckled web carries the load in diagonal tension; failure is yielding of the web or failure of a flange or stiffener.
Forgetting the flange compression W/(2 tan α). Both flanges lose 11.6 kN of tension in the example: the compression flange is more loaded than bending alone says.
Using sin α cos α = 1 at 45°. It is 0.5; dropping it gives half the true σ<sub>t</sub>, an unsafe error.
Designing the stiffeners for no load. In a tension field they are struts carrying W b tan α/d and must not buckle.

quiz.q: Write Wagner's expression for the diagonal tension stress in a complete tension field.
quiz.a: σ<sub>t</sub> = 2W/(t d sin 2α): W the shear (N), t the web thickness (mm), d the depth between flanges (mm), α the angle of the field to the flanges.

quiz.q: What is a shear-resistant web beam?
quiz.a: A beam whose web is stiff enough to carry the whole shear without buckling, so the ordinary shear flow q = W/d applies.

quiz.q: Why do the wrinkles of a buckled web run along one diagonal?
quiz.a: Pure shear equals tension on one diagonal and compression on the other. The thin web buckles under the compression and keeps carrying the tension, so the folds line up with the tension diagonal.

quiz.q: For the example beam at α = 45°, find σ<sub>t</sub>, the stiffener load and the extra flange compression.
A web 400 mm deep and 1.2 mm thick carries 60 kN. Find the nominal shear stress.
In the example the stiffeners are made much stiffer (A<sub>S</sub> → ∞). What happens to α and to the stiffener load?
quiz.a: tan⁴α = 1.4, tan α = 1.0878 and α = 47.4°. The stiffener load rises to 16,316 N, because a steeper field pulls the flanges together harder.

quiz.q: Why are aircraft webs allowed to buckle in service?
quiz.a: A web thick enough not to buckle would be several times heavier. The flanges and stiffeners are there anyway; making them carry the tension field costs little, so the buckled web is the lighter design. The price is lower stiffness, flange secondary bending and fatigue at the wrinkles.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real transport aircraft webs are designed by incomplete tension field methods that include the buckling stress, curved panels and rivet loads. Search for "incomplete diagonal tension field" and "tension field beam".
